name: The Winner's Curse
statement: The auction winner is the one who most overestimated the prize — and so overpaid.
meaning: In a common-value auction under uncertainty — where the item is worth roughly the same to everyone but nobody knows exactly what — the winning bidder tends to overpay. The winner is disproportionately likely to be the bidder who most overestimated the value, so winning is itself bad news about your own estimate. A rational bidder must therefore shade their bid below their raw estimate to correct for this.
mechanism: Suppose a single unknown value is common to all bidders, and each forms an independent, error-laden estimate of it. Even if every estimate is unbiased on its own, the highest of several estimates is biased upward — the maximum of noisy guesses tends to overshoot the truth. A first-price auction hands the item to roughly the highest estimator, so the winner's estimate was probably too high. The more bidders, the worse the overshoot. The rational response is to condition on the very event of winning, which lowers the value you should expect, and to bid below your estimate accordingly.

examples.text: The idea was born from offshore oil-lease bidding, where companies won leases but earned poor returns year after year, because the winner was systematically the over-optimistic bidder.
The acquirer's curse: competitive bidding for a company of uncertain worth leads the winner to overpay, a common explanation for why acquisitions so often destroy value.
From radio-spectrum licence auctions to bidding wars over free-agent athletes of uncertain future performance, the most optimistic bidder wins the shared-value prize and overpays.

variants.name: Bid shading
variants.text: The rational correction: bidding strictly below your raw estimate, by an amount that grows with the number of competitors and the noise in your signal, so that in equilibrium expected profit is not negative.

variants.name: Common versus private value
variants.text: The curse arises only in common-value auctions, where the item is worth the same to all; in pure private-value auctions, where each bidder has an idiosyncratic valuation, winning conveys no bad news and the curse does not apply.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational result of auction theory and a sharp lesson in conditional reasoning: that winning a competitive bid is informative, and usually bad news, about your own valuation. It explains chronic overpayment across oil leases, takeovers, spectrum sales, and sports contracts, and it shaped the design of real auctions, work recognised by the 2020 Nobel in economics.

working.text: in a common-value auction, bid below your raw estimate, more so the more rivals there are and the noisier your information.
ask what the item is worth given that your bid was the highest, not just what your estimate says, since winning signals over-optimism.
apply the curse only where value is common and uncertain, not to pure private-value auctions.

limits: The curse requires both a common-value component and genuine uncertainty about that value; it does not apply to pure private-value auctions, and it weakens as uncertainty shrinks. Laboratory studies find even experienced bidders fall prey to it — construction executives did about as badly as students, apparently because their field rules of thumb do not transfer to the lab — so whether experience cures it is mixed. And its magnitude in real markets is contested and hard to identify cleanly, being far better documented in the laboratory than in the field.
misreadings: The winner's curse is not the same as merely overpaying or feeling buyer's remorse — it is specifically the statistical selection effect that winning correlates with having the most over-optimistic estimate. It is not simple irrationality either: a bidder who shades correctly avoids it, and only one who fails to condition on winning suffers it. It does not apply to private-value auctions, where overbidding, when it occurs, is a different phenomenon. And the winner does not always literally lose money; the claim is a tendency toward overpayment on average.
origin: Described by three petroleum engineers, Capen, Clapp, and Campbell, in 'Competitive Bidding in High-Risk Situations' (Journal of Petroleum Technology, 1971) from oil-lease bidding; formalised in auction theory by Wilson and by Milgrom and Weber, and popularised by Richard Thaler.

sources.text: Capen, Clapp & Campbell, "Competitive Bidding in High-Risk Situations," Journal of Petroleum Technology 23:641-653 (1971). — the original account from oil-lease bidding.
Thaler, "Anomalies: The Winner's Curse," Journal of Economic Perspectives 2(1):191-202 (1988). — the survey that popularised the effect.

Dyer, Kagel & Levin, "A Comparison of Naive and Experienced Bidders in Common Value Offer Auctions," Economic Journal 99(394):108-115 (1989). — experienced bidders falling prey to the curse in the laboratory.
